hints: Picture the starting point as completely separated ions in the gas phase, not a solid or aqueous ions.
Remember to specify the amount of solid made and the conditions that make the value standard.
walkthrough:
Fix the starting particles in your mind**
Think of $\text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{g})$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}(\text{g})$ flying freely and far apart. Lattice formation is those gaseous ions coming together to lock into the giant lattice $\text{CuCl}_{2}(\text{s})$. It is not from solid elements or from aqueous ions.

Add the amount and conditions**
Cambridge always wants the quantity and the standard state. State 1 mole of solid formed, and add under standard conditions ($298 \text{ K}$, $101 \text{ kPa}$). That gives the full definition and both marks.
Final answer: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of an ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions under standard conditions.

hints: Draw a Hess cycle with solid going up to gaseous ions then down to aqueous ions, so solution = reverse lattice plus hydrations.
Check the formula $\text{CuCl}_{2}$ carefully to see how many moles of $\text{Cl}^{-}$ hydration you need.
walkthrough:
Build the energy route**
Dissolving has two stages. First break the lattice apart, which is the reverse of lattice formation, so $-\Delta H_{latt} = +2824 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Then hydrate the gaseous ions, which is exothermic. By Hess's law: $$\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_{latt} + \Sigma \Delta H_{hyd}$$

Substitute with the factor of 2**
One mole of $\text{CuCl}_{2}$ gives one $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ but two $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions, so only the chloride hydration is doubled: $$\Delta H_{sol} = (-2099) + (2 \times -378) - (-2824)$$ $$= -2099 -756 +2824 = -31 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Keep the sign and units $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Final answer: $$\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_{latt} + \Delta H_{hyd}(\text{Cu}^{2+}) + 2\Delta H_{hyd}(\text{Cl}^{-})$$
$$= -(-2824) + (-2099) + 2(-378) = -31 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

hints: Compare the sizes of $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ using ionic radii from the Data Booklet, both ions have the same charge.
Link a smaller ion with the same charge to how strongly it can pull on the partial negative oxygen of water.
walkthrough:
Compare charge density**
Both ions are 2+, so charge is identical. The difference must be size. $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is much smaller than $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, so the same 2+ charge is packed into a smaller volume. That means higher charge density.

Link to attraction for water**
Hydration is the attraction of gaseous ions for the $\delta-$ oxygen end of water. A smaller, more concentrated charge pulls water molecules closer and forms stronger ion-dipole attractions, releasing more energy. Hence $\Delta H_{hyd}$ for $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ($-2099 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) is far more negative than for $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ ($-1579 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$).

Final answer: $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ so has a higher charge density.
$\text{Cu}^{2+}$ attracts water molecules more strongly, forming stronger ion-dipole forces, so hydration is more exothermic.

hints: List the ions present from $\text{CaCl}_{2}$ plus water, then recall which ion is preferentially discharged at each electrode in concentrated chloride solution.
walkthrough:
Sort the competing discharges**
In solution you have $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ from the salt plus $\text{H}^{+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ from water. At the cathode $\text{H}^{+}$ (water) discharges in preference to very reactive $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, giving $\text{H}_{2}$. At the anode, because the solution is saturated (concentrated) in $\text{Cl}^{-}$, chloride discharges in preference to $\text{OH}^{-}$, giving $\text{Cl}_{2}$.

Final answer: at the anode: chlorine, $\text{Cl}_{2}$
at the cathode: hydrogen, $\text{H}_{2}$

hints: Start with $Q = It$ and remember to convert the 60 minutes into seconds to get charge in coulombs.
Write the cathode half equation $\text{Ca}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ca}$ to find how many moles of electrons make one mole of Ca.
walkthrough:
Find the total charge and moles of electrons**
Charge is current times time in seconds: $$Q = It = 0.75 \times 3600 = 2700 \text{ C}$$ One mole of electrons carries $96500 \text{ C}$, so moles $e^{-} = 2700/96500$.

Convert electrons to calcium mass**
Calcium needs two electrons per atom: $\text{Ca}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ca}(\text{l})$. So divide by 2, equivalent to dividing charge by $2 \times 96500 = 193000$: $$n(\text{Ca}) = 2700/193000 = 0.0140 \text{ mol}$$ Then mass $= n \times A_{r} = 0.0140 \times 40.1 = 0.56 \text{ g}$ (2 s.f.).

Final answer: $$Q = 0.75 \times 60 \times 60 = 2700 \text{ C}$$
$$\text{moles Ca} = 2700 / 193000 = 0.0140$$
$$\text{mass} = 0.0140 \times 40.1 = 0.56 \text{ g}$$

hints: Think of entropy as a count of how spread out and disordered the particles and their energy can be.
walkthrough:
Picture disorder**
Forget complicated maths. Entropy $S$ simply tells you how disordered a system is. A gas with particles moving freely has many ways to arrange itself, so high entropy. A perfect crystal has few ways, so low entropy. Stating disorder or number of arrangements earns the mark.
Final answer: A measure of the degree of disorder or randomness of a system, or the number of possible arrangements of particles and their energy.

hints: Compare order before and after: solid to mobile ions versus freely moving liquid to fixed lattice.
walkthrough:
Judge order change**
Dissolving $\text{NaCl}(\text{s})$ releases ordered lattice ions into mobile aqueous ions, so disorder increases and $\Delta S$ is positive. Freezing liquid water locks mobile molecules into a fixed hydrogen bonded ice lattice, so disorder decreases and $\Delta S$ is negative.

Final answer: $\text{NaCl}$ dissolving in water: $\Delta S$ is positive.
water solidifying to ice: $\Delta S$ is negative.

hints: Recall $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ and that evaporation has positive $\Delta S$, so the $-T\Delta S$ term makes $\Delta G$ fall as T rises.
Think about the temperature where liquid water and steam are in equilibrium at 101 kPa, where $\Delta G^{\ominus} = 0$.
walkthrough:
Set the start and slope**
At $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ plot $+8.6 \text{ kJ}$ on the positive $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ axis. Evaporation $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}(\text{l}) \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}\text{O}(\text{g})$ increases disorder so $\Delta S$ is positive. From $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, as $T$ rises the $T\Delta S$ term grows, so $\Delta G$ must decrease steadily, giving a line of negative gradient.

Fix the crossing point**
At the normal boiling point, liquid and gas are in equilibrium so $\Delta G^{\ominus} = 0$. At $101 \text{ kPa}$ this is about $100^{\circ}\text{C}$. Draw a straight or gently curved line falling through zero at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ into the negative region by $150^{\circ}\text{C}$, showing evaporation becomes feasible at high T.

Final answer: Line starts at $+8.6 \text{ kJ}$ (positive $\Delta G^{\ominus}$) at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$, slopes downwards with negative gradient, crosses the temperature axis at about $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ and continues negative to $150^{\circ}\text{C}$.

hints: Use $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ and test which sign combination gives negative $\Delta G$ at low T but positive $\Delta G$ at high T.
Consider that at low T the $\Delta H$ term dominates, while at high T the $T\Delta S$ term dominates.
walkthrough:
Deduce the signs**
Feasible means $\Delta G < 0$. With $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, the only way to be negative at low T but positive at high T is both terms negative. $\Delta H$ must be negative (exothermic favours feasibility) and $\Delta S$ must be negative (so $-T\Delta S = +T|\Delta S|$ opposes feasibility and grows with T).

Explain the switch with temperature**
At low temperature, $T\Delta S$ is small, so the negative $\Delta H$ wins and $\Delta G$ is negative. As temperature rises, the positive $+T|\Delta S|$ term gets larger until it outweighs $\Delta H$, making $\Delta G$ positive. That is why the reaction stops being feasible on heating.

Final answer: sign of $\Delta H$ = negative, sign of $\Delta S$ = negative.
At low T, $\Delta H$ is more negative than $T\Delta S$ so $\Delta G$ is negative and feasible. At high T, $T\Delta S$ dominates so $\Delta G$ becomes positive and not feasible.
